ECONOMICS

  • Economics is the study of how people, businesses, and governments use limited resources to produce, distribute, and consume goods and services.
  • Economics broadly divided into: Macroeconomics and Microeconomics.
AspectsMacroeconomicsMicroeconomics
DefinitionIt studies the economy as a wholeIt studies individual consumers, firms, and markets
Focus AreaIt is focused on the action of government and countries that take to influence broader economics like supply, demand, prices, etc.It is focused with the action of individual or businesses
ScopeLarge-scale, entire economySmall-scale, specific sector
FatherJ. M. Keynes (from England) wrote the "General Theory of Employment, Interest and money"Adam Smith (Founding Father of Modern Economy) wrote the book "The wealth of Nations"
ExamplesGDP, inflation rates, fiscal policies, national income, unemployment ratesPricing of a product, consumer behavior, competition in a market

The economic system can be classified into three types:

  1. 1. Capitalist Economy
  2. 2. Socialist Economy
  3. 3. Mixed Economy
CapitalistSocialistMixed
OwnershipPrivate ownershipPublic ownershipPublic + Private ownership
Economic motiveProfitSocial welfareBoth
Government roleNo roleComplete involvementLimited role
Income distributionUnequalEqualLess unequal
Economic freedomCompleteLack of freedomLimited freedom
ExampleUSAUSSR, North KoreaIndia

Licence Raj and LPG Reforms 1991

  • Licence Raj, also called "Permit Raj", was a system in India before 1991 where businesses had to get many government approvals to start or run.
  • During this time, the government controlled industries, imports, and trade, which slowed down the country's growth and caused economic crisis. India faced a Balance of Payment (BoP) crisis with very little foreign exchange reserve left.
  • To solve this, LPG reforms 1991 (Liberalization, Privatization, Globalization) was introduced, it was led by Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh, this reform made doing business easier and opened up the Indian economy to the world.

Rivalrous Goods

A good is said to be rivalrous if its consumption by one consumer prevents simultaneous consumption by other consumers.

Difference between Public Goods and Private Goods

Private GoodsPublic Goods
They are rivalrous (provide satisfaction to only limited persons)They are non-rivalrous (provide satisfaction to all)
They are excludable (E.g. A person can exclude someone from sitting in the car)They are non-excludable (E.g. Any person can use the public bridge)
They are generally provided by Private Sector (made by a private car company)They are generally provided by the Government (public provisions made by Government)
They have a positive marginal costs.They have zero marginal costs.

Public goods involve the problem of Free Ridership (Bole to: Muft ka Chandan Ghis Mere Nandan).

SECTORS OF ECONOMY

There are three sectors of economy:

  1. 1. Primary Sector
  2. 2. Secondary Sector
  3. 3. Tertiary Sector

Primary Sector

  • This sector is directly dependent on the environment.
  • In India Primary Sector is mostly seen in agricultural activities. E.g. Agriculture, Fishing, Hunting, Forestry, Mining.
  • The types of activities under this sector is also known as Red Collar Jobs.

Agriculture Sector is considered "the backbone of Indian Economy"

Secondary Sector

  • It is also called as Manufacturing Sector.
  • They add value to natural resources by transforming raw materials into valuable products. E.g. Manufacturing, processing, building/construction, electricity etc.
  • Secondary Sector is considered backbone of a country, as it helps in industrialisation of a country. E.g. China.
  • Secondary Sector is also known as Blue Collar Jobs and is yet not developed in India properly. We have directly leaped to Tertiary Sector.

Tertiary Sector

  • It is also known as Service Sector.
  • It is a part of economy where business produce services. E.g. Teaching, Transport, Advertising, Retail, Hospitality and Healthcare.
  • It is always intangible (something which cannot be touched) in nature.
  • It is also known as White Collar Jobs.

Blue-collar jobs involve physical work and use practical skills. These jobs are often in fields like construction, manufacturing, and maintenance.

Quaternary Sector

  • The Quaternary Sector focuses on knowledge-based activities and intellectual services.
  • This sector is also known as the "Knowledge Sector". E.g. Senior Business Executive, Teaching, Manager, Banking, Chartered Accountant, Lawyer, Scientists.

Quinary Sector

  • The Quinary Sector involves high-level, knowledge-based activities that require expertise and advanced skills → All the decision making activities are involved here.
  • The activities in this sector are also known as Gold Collar Jobs. E.g. Media, Financial Services, Education, Research Scientists, Information Technology, Activity of Politicians.

LFPR: Labour Force Participation Rate

  • Percentage of women engaged in Primary Sector: 62.8%

Aids or Auxiliaries to Trade

  • Auxiliaries to trade refers to the factors that are essential for bringing the goods from the place of their production to the place of their consumption. In other words, these are essential services and functions that assist the business. E.g. Transportation, communication, banking, insurance, warehousing, and advertising.

Normative Vs Positive Economics

Normative EconomicsPositive Economics
It is based on opinion and value of the interpreterIt is based on actual data, facts, and numbers
Verification is not possibleResults can be verified
No way to test feasibility and applicability in various fieldSafe and beyond doubt and can be proved scientifically
It deals with idealistic situationIt deals with actual and realistic situations
E.g. The level of unemployment must be 5% maximum.E.g. The current unemployment rate is 20%.

Parallel Economy

  • Parallel Economy refers to all the forms of activities through which black income is generated and those which are usually not accounted.
  • It renders Policies by Government Ineffective.
